---
title: "Allocating yield trial plots"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

Every breeding program has a fixed number of plots, and every year it decides
how to spend them. Test more lines at fewer locations, or fewer lines at more
locations? Add a second rep, or a second location? This is one of the oldest
questions in plant breeding, and the answer depends on things specific to
your program: how large genotype-by-environment (G×E) interaction is, how
heritable a single plot is, and how many lines you can afford to make.

This article answers it for a soybean-style line pipeline with
`line_pipeline()`, a ready-made AlphaSimR program, without writing any
AlphaSimR code.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## The pipeline

`line_pipeline()` simulates the pipeline most self-pollinated crop programs
run. Each cycle, it crosses the parents and advances the progeny to inbred
lines by single-seed descent. Every line goes into a preliminary yield trial
(PYT), and the best `n_ayt` lines go on to an advanced yield trial (AYT). The
best AYT lines are released and recycled as parents.

```{r}
pipeline <- line_pipeline(
  n_crosses = 30, progeny_per_cross = 20,     # 600 new lines per cycle
  n_parents = 20, n_release = 5, cycles = 2,
  n_ayt = tune(), ayt_locations = tune(), ayt_reps = tune(),
  founders = asr_founders(n_chr = 10, seg_sites = 100, plot_h2 = 0.3)
)
pipeline
```

The AYT has 480 plots. Every way of splitting them is a design: 480 lines at
one location with one rep, 240 lines at two locations, 60 lines at four
locations with two reps, and so on. We list them ourselves, so that every
design uses the whole budget:

```{r}
budget <- 480
designs <- expand.grid(ayt_locations = c(1, 2, 4, 8), ayt_reps = c(1, 2))
designs$n_ayt <- budget / (designs$ayt_locations * designs$ayt_reps)
designs
```

## Two assumptions about G×E

How much G×E your environments have is an *assumption*, not a choice. We
don't know it exactly, so we run every design under two values. `gxe_var` is
the G×E variance as a fraction of the founders' genetic variance:

```{r}
reps <- sim_replicates(15, seed = 1, scenarios = sim_scenarios(gxe_var = c(0.2, 1)))
reps
```

## Run it

```{r}
metrics <- sim_metric_set(release_gain, sim_metric("ayt_accuracy", "maximize"), plots)
res <- tune_grid(pipeline, reps, grid = designs, metrics = metrics)
res
```

`r nrow(designs)` designs × 2 scenarios × 15 replicates is
`r nrow(designs) * 2 * 15` simulated breeding programs, written in one call.

## Locations or reps?

```{r, fig.alt = "Gain of released lines against number of AYT locations, one line per number of reps, in two panels for low and high G×E."}
m <- collect_metrics(res, by_scenario = TRUE, type = "wide")
m$gxe <- ifelse(m$.scenario == "gxe_var=0.2", "Low GxE (0.2)", "High GxE (1)")
ggplot(m, aes(ayt_locations, release_gain, colour = factor(ayt_reps))) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = release_gain - release_gain_se, ymax = release_gain + release_gain_se),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  facet_wrap(~gxe) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log2", breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 8)) +
  labs(x = "AYT locations (fewer lines as you go right)", y = "Gain of released lines",
       colour = "Reps per location", title = "Spending 480 AYT plots")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Accuracy of AYT means against number of locations, one line per number of reps, for low and high G×E."}
ggplot(m, aes(ayt_locations, ayt_accuracy, colour = factor(ayt_reps))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~gxe) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log2", breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 8)) +
  labs(x = "AYT locations", y = "Accuracy of AYT means", colour = "Reps per location")
```

Read the two plots together:

* **Accuracy** rises with the number of plots each line gets. For the same
  plots per line, spreading them over more locations is at least as accurate
  as adding reps, and slightly more so when G×E is high, because only new
  environments average G×E away.
* **Gain** needs accuracy *and* enough lines to select among. Testing all 480
  lines at one location is the worst design in both scenarios: lots of lines,
  but they are ranked so poorly that selection barely helps. Going to the
  other extreme, 30 lines at 16 plots each, gives up too much selection
  intensity. The best designs test 60 to 120 lines with 4 to 8 plots each,
  spread over 2 to 8 locations.
* **The top designs are close.** Their averages are within about one
  standard error of each other, so the simulation cannot separate them with
  15 replicates. That is useful too: choose among them on cost and
  logistics (a new location usually costs more than a second rep), or run
  more replicates for just those designs.

Scenarios show how much the answer depends on what you assumed. Here the
ranking of the top designs shifts a little between low and high G×E, but the
main lesson, to give each AYT line several environments, holds in both.

```{r}
show_best(res, metric = "release_gain", scenario = "gxe_var=1", n = 3)
show_best(res, metric = "release_gain", scenario = "gxe_var=0.2", n = 3)
```

## Make it yours

Everything above is one spec and one call to `tune_grid()`. To fit it to
your program, change the arguments:

* **Your budget and costs:** `plot_cost`, `cross_cost`, `ssd_cost`, and
  `max_plots` or `max_cost` to rule out designs over budget.
* **Your pipeline:** `n_crosses`, `progeny_per_cross`, `line_generation`,
  `generations_per_year` (2 with a winter nursery), `pyt_locations`,
  `n_parents`.
* **Your trait:** `plot_h2` and `gxe_var`, best set from your own trial data
  and run as scenarios when you are unsure.
* **Let the tuner choose:** mark any of these `tune()` and use `tune_bayes()`
  to search a large space, as in [Choosing a design](choosing-designs.html).
